speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As part of this review, we introduced the Criminal Justice Reform Act 2018 (CJRA) last year, which amended the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) and other laws.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The scale of the current Bill is much smaller than that of CJRA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The current proposals serve to improve and refine the laws introduced or amended last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments can be split into three main categories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, investigative processes; second, Court procedure; and third, the sentencing powers of the Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The first change to investigative processes concerns video-recording of interviews (VRI).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When we implemented VRI last year, we also created new offences relating to the misuse of VRI recordings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Examples include the unauthorised recording of the VRI process and the unauthorised copying or distribution of a VRI statement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The existing law allows the Police to investigate such VRI-related offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, other agencies that use VRI in their investigations may not have the power to investigate such offences and would have to rely on the Police to investigate them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, if the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) is conducting a drug-related investigation and takes a VRI recording, and that recording is wrongfully copied or distributed, the CNB cannot investigate that act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It must call on the Police to assist with that aspect of the investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The law enforcement agencies gave us feedback that it would be a lot more efficient if the investigative agency that makes a VRI recording was empowered to investigate any misuse of that recording.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That agency would be familiar with the wider investigation and would be able to put the VRI-related offence into its proper context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The intention is to prescribe CNB as such an agency, with others considered as and when the need arises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Sensitive information refers to information which, if disclosed: (a) may be prejudicial to the public safety, public security or propriety, public order, national interest or national security of Singapore or any part of Singapore; (b) may endanger the safety of any particular person; (c) may prejudice the effective conduct of any ongoing or future operation or investigation of any law enforcement agency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, information that may reveal the operational processes or capabilities of any law enforcement agency; or (d) may otherwise be prejudicial to the interests of justice in any criminal investigation or criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our current statutes already provide for the non-disclosure of official records relating to affairs of state and, in certain circumstances, official communications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The proposed amendment, which applies only in the criminal context, expressly allows a law enforcement officer or the Prosecution to redact sensitive information if, for example, the redaction is needed to protect a person's safety or the effective conduct of an investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To take a further example, let us say that CNB takes a VRI statement from a suspect, who is a member of a drug trafficking syndicate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the course of the interview, it is revealed that CNB has certain intelligence-gathering capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If this part of the video-recording were to be publicly disclosed, it could compromise CNB’s intelligence-gathering and undermine investigations not just into that syndicate, but also others as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The proposed amendments would expressly allow that part of the VRI statement to be redacted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We were, of course, mindful that any exercise of this power should not prejudice an accused person's ability to conduct their defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A key objective of the criminal justice system is to produce accurate and equitable outcomes, through procedures that are fair, and not just fair but seen to be fair as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With this in mind, the power to redact comes with certain limitations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Prosecution will not be allowed to redact sensitive information from material disclosed to the Defence (a) where the Prosecution intends to rely on that sensitive information as evidence, or (b) where the law requires the disclosure of the sensitive information because it tends to undermine the Prosecution’s case or to strengthen the defence's case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This latter type of disclosure refers to the principle in the Court of Appeal’s decision in Muhammad bin Kadar and another v Public Prosecutor and the cases that elaborate on that decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the Defence wishes to dispute a redaction made under this power, the amendments provide that they may apply to the Court in a closed-door hearing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Court will view the material in the absence of the Defence and it may order that the Prosecution disclose the redacted information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I turn now to cover an amendment relating to Court procedure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: CJRA introduced a statutory procedure for reopening concluded criminal cases, where all avenues of appeal have been exhausted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the CJRA amendments, the appellate Court that last dealt with the case will hear the application to reopen the case and may extend certain timelines for filing documents prescribed for the reopening procedure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Again, we received feedback that it would be more efficient, and also allow more flexibility for the Courts, if this procedural power includes the power both to shorten and extend timelines, and if it can be exercised not only by the last appellate Court to hear the matter, but also the Registrar of the Supreme Court, and any High Court Judge or Judge of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are, therefore, proposing an amendment to that effect.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: RT sentences apply to offenders under the age of 21.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under such sentences, young people who commit relatively serious crimes go through intensive rehabilitation in a Reformative Training Centre (RTC) followed by post-detention supervision in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The RT regime is specifically geared towards the rehabilitation of young offenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It emphasises both discipline and rehabilitation in a structured environment, where officers provide supervision and guidance to the RT trainees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The trainees will go through programmes that will help them take charge of their rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They will need to soberly reflect on their offences, on how to stay crime-free, and on how to strengthen their relationships with their family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under CJRA, the CPC was amended last year to reduce the minimum RT detention period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This substantial reduction in the minimum detention period benefits offenders because it allows them to return to the community and begin their social reintegration earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the reduced period also means that offenders have a very limited time in RTC to complete the intensive rehabilitative programmes designed to keep them crime-free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If an RT sentence is shortened any further by backdating, it would deprive the offender of the chance to complete the necessary programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Without the full benefits of their rehabilitation, there is a higher risk that the offender will not be able to stay crime-free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will not be good for them or society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are conscious that with this amendment, an offender who is remanded for a substantial period of time before being sentenced to RT will face a longer total period of incarceration compared to an offender who was not remanded or not remanded for as long.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This was a concern raised by the criminal Bar during our consultation with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Of course, this is leaving aside remand ordered by the sentencing Court for preparing the RT pre-sentencing report, which agencies currently keep to about one week or less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These clarify the Court's procedure and powers in forfeiting bail bonds, introduce definitions to aid understanding of the High Court criminal case disclosure procedure and improve some language which was unclear.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To conclude, the Bill builds on the reforms in the CJRA of last year and further enhances the effectiveness of some of those reforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In this modest way, it contributes towards a fair criminal justice system that serves the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, on VRIs, I must commend the Ministry on how far it has moved on VRI over the years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I first broached the idea of video-recording of statements during the Ministry of Law's (MinLaw's) Committee of Supply (COS) in 2008, more than 10 years ago, it was met with a negative response.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, we are here discussing how to enhance the VRI framework to cover law enforcement officers outside of the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill seeks to enable non-Police officers to investigate offences relating to a statement made by an audiovisual recording.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The rationale for this change was explained in MinLaw's press release of 11 February, as to enable CNB officers who had used video-recorded interviews as part of their investigations to be able to investigate VRI-related offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to which types of cases are being investigated with the use of VRI, section 22 of the CPC currently makes VRI mandatory only in cases of rape under section 375(1)(a) of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Also, what has been the assessment thus far of the usefulness of VRI as an investigation tool and as evidence in Court?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, backdating a sentence to start running at an earlier date could happen if the offender was remanded in custody from the time of his arrest and continued to be in custody for weeks or months before he is eventually sentenced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such backdating recognises that he has lost his liberty from an earlier date, and takes that pre-sentence period into account.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MinLaw has explained that it is removing the possibility of backdating sentences of RT because RT is geared towards rehabilitation and if sentences are backdated, the offenders may not have enough time to complete the prescribed programmes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That I understand is due to the changes made to RT over the years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But when backdating does not happen, how do we account to the individual for the period he or she has spent in pre-sentence custody?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not backdating may cause injustice to the offender.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I see that MinLaw is alive to this injustice as, in its media release, it has stated that agencies will work together to ensure that where RT is a likely sentence, remand is avoided or minimised where possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As RT will be imposed on young offenders, namely, those below 21, it is certainly important to ensure that these youths are not incarcerated for longer than necessary, as it would affect their reintegration into education, society and work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, will the prosecution be more prepared to ask for lower bail amounts, or will the cases be fast tracked in a specific way?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be important for the Ministry to clarify that such post-dating would only occur if the offender is not incarcerated while waiting to commence a sentence of RT.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is good as it streamlines the process by allowing the agency which is most familiar with the circumstance to investigate the offence, thereby smoothening the process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to fulfil such duties, is it envisioned that the skillsets and expertise will be slightly different from what the officers from the prescribed law enforcement agency are already using?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, what training or arrangements will be provided to ensure that the officers would be able to develop the necessary expertise to tap into the requisite resources to investigate each case?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Still staying on this issue, why does the new section 40B remove the need for an officer to be of an equivalent rank to that of an Inspector of the Police without seemingly replacing it with an equivalent safeguard?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me, Sir, at this stage, to declare my interest as a lawyer in private practice who sometimes acts as Defence counsel.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, while sensitive information may prejudice public safety, safety of any particular person or future investigations, the prosecution may still need to disclose it if it is required by law and if it undermines the prosecution’s case or strengthens the Defence's case according to the new section 425B(3).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, by the words "if the Defence is aggrieved by the removal or redaction" in the new section 425B(4), it seems as though the Court’s determination on the matter can be easily sought by the Defence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While not allowing the Defence to be present as the Court views the document makes sense in order for this non-disclosure to be effective, would this be an exception to Rule 30 of the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules 2015 under which legal practitioners are ethically bound not to initiate any communication with the Court unless he or she has given each legal practitioner acting for another party to the proceedings an opportunity to be present or to reply?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is my question to the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, how does the process take into account the general understanding that the Defence would be best placed to know whether something would strengthen its own case?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another question, these concerns must be weighed against the importance of protecting sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The provision could protect public safety, public security or propriety, public order, national interest, national security, safety of individuals, ongoing and future investigations and interest of justice in criminal investigation or proceedings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as the accused must be able to present the best case, such important concerns cannot be compromised if there is no need to, especially if it does not weaken the prosecution’s case or strengthen the Defence's case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, when there is a need to disclose such information even though it is sensitive information, what will be done to safeguard the sensitive information from being abused?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, how can we be sure that information is, indeed, disclosed even where it is valuable or relevant and necessary to the Defence's case?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Post-trial, certain timings for both the application for leave of review application as well as the hearing of a review application can be abridged through clauses 7 and 8.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As these two powers would be able to shorten the timeline from those prescribed in the Criminal Procedure Rules, potentially prejudicing the relevant parties, would the Senior Minister of State please explain the rationale behind these amendments?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The fourth area of substantive amendments that I want to speak about in this very short speech is that of RT.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The RT regime is an important feature of our criminal justice system through both rehabilitation and deterrence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this removes the period that the accused was remanded for pre-sentencing, this amendment furthers the aim and purpose of RT.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, this amendment will promote the effectiveness of the RT regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Following CJRA 2018 which allowed for a more calibrated rehabilitation programme through changes to the duration of the RT regime, this amendment will further enhance the effectiveness of RT and is a welcomed amendment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, what will be done to ensure that the duration of remand will be reduced or minimised?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, since corrective training (CT) also contains rehabilitation as part of its focus, did the Ministry consider introducing a similar change to disallow backdating for CT and, if so, why was it not extended to CT?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The CPC is integral to our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to achieve justice in our criminal justice system, the process must be robust yet flexible, balanced and fair.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has to take into account both the interests of not just the accused, not just the victim but also that of the broader society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked if non-Police law enforcement officers will need different skills, training and resources to investigate these offences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This workgroup will work towards ensuring that the investigation of VRI offences is done to a common high standard across all agencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked why the non-Police Officers exercising the new powers to investigate VRI offences do not need to be of a rank equivalent to an Inspector of Police but are deemed to be of that rank for these purposes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is to match the existing powers of those officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, under section 32 of the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA), a CNB officer investigating an offence under that Act has the same CPC powers as a Police Officer investigating an arrestable offence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In exercising those powers, the CNB officer is deemed by section 32(3) to be an officer not below the rank of Inspector of Police.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Provisions like section 32 of the MDA and the proposed section 40B of the CPC recognise the fact that officers of specialised law enforcement agencies, such as CNB, are highly trained and are able to competently and responsibly exercise the investigative powers given to Police Officers of the rank of Inspector and above.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked which agencies have commenced using VRI, for what kinds of offences, and for the assessment of the usefulness of VRI in investigations and as evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several Police land divisions are also preparing to use VRI.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As more cases go through the criminal justice system, we will continue to gather feedback from the implementing agencies in order to further refine and improve the VRI process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With reference to the suggestion in 2008, that MinLaw was dismissive of this during COS, let me just clarify the position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The answer then was that MHA will take ownership of this issue and, at that stage, whilst MHA had no plans to implement VRI, they were nonetheless, and I quote, "MHA's position is that the issue of video recording as well as other operational issues should be looked into, in the following manner: there should be a fair system which seeks to ensure that crimes are solved and the system should also ensure that the rights of the accused are protected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If an accused wishes to challenge the statement given by him, there are clear avenues available today".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that was the position in 2008, not quite so dismissive as Ms Sylvia Lim has suggested.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, there were several questions on the removal of sensitive information from disclosed materials.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked if the Defence can easily seek the Court’s determination of whether such a removal or redaction should stand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, leave of Court will not be required.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, to succeed, the Defence will need to satisfy the Court that the Prosecution should not have redacted the relevant information, either because it was not sensitive information, because the Prosecution is relying on it as evidence, or because it tends to assist the Defence or undermine the Prosecution’s case and, therefore, must be legally disclosed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether the requirement that the Court view the disputed redacted material in the absence of the Defence violates an ethical rule against a party communicating with the Court without the other party also being present or able to reply, I would like to make it clear that the rules of natural justice will continue to apply to those proceedings just as they have done in other proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This means that both parties will be able to make submissions on the legality of the redaction and also rebut each other's submissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While the Court must view the disputed material in the absence of the Defence, this does not mean that the Prosecution will be allowed to make submissions in the absence of the Defence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, you make the submissions, the Defence can respond and the Court views the disputed material in the absence of the Defence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked how this procedure takes into account the understanding that the Defence would be best placed to know whether something would strengthen its own case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This question relates to the common law principle from the case of Kadar, which I mentioned earlier, that the Prosecution must disclose unused material that tends to strengthen the Defence's case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza's question calls to mind the argument, sometimes advanced before the Courts, that the Defence should receive disclosure of material for the purposes of arguing that it should be disclosed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The High Court, in fact, considered this precise point in Winston Lee's case and held that even where it fell to the Prosecution to show that in compliance with its Kadar disclosure obligations, the disputed material may be shown to the Court but not to the Defence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, to quote the judgment on this, " o allow the Defence to examine the undisclosed material on a preliminary basis simply because there is a dispute on disclosability has a similar practical effect to disclosure and this would in essence be going further than the situations of disclosure envisaged in  ".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The wording in the proposed legislation is entirely consistent with this commonsense position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a similar vein, Mr Christopher de Souza asked how we can be sure that information is, indeed, disclosed where it is valuable or relevant and necessary to the Defence's case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the Defence assisting the Court in this regard, we are confident that the outcomes will be fair when the Kadar principles are applied in the context of the redaction of sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Prosecution will weigh very carefully, in the first place, whether to use sensitive information as part of its evidence, and will only do so where it is necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If unredacted sensitive information has to be used in a criminal proceeding, various measures can be taken to mitigate the risk of publicity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, if there is sensitive information in materials disclosed in the statutory pre-trial disclosure process, the Court may order that the accused and his advocate cannot communicate it to any person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Breach of this order would be an offence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also worth noting that, generally, the media are not allowed to publish reports of information contained in materials disclosed during the statutory pre-trial disclosure process, except the basic facts of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the Court may order that the matter be heard behind closed doors – in camera.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is commonly known as a "gag order".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moving to the next area being amended, Mr Christopher de Souza asked for the rationale of giving the Courts and the Registrar the power to shorten timelines in relation to procedure for reopening of concluded cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I should highlight that both parties will be given a chance to make arguments about the timelines before the Court makes the decision to either shorten or extend them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that is the usual way where the Court will entertain submissions from both parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court will take on board all the facts and arguments, taking them into account in deciding whether it is, in fact, just to make the order or not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I stated in my opening speech that this proposal was designed to enhance efficiency and allow for more flexibility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Let us say an application to reopen a concluded case is filed very late and close to the time the sentence is to be carried out, for example, a caning sentence, which will be irremediable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With this amendment, the Court will be able to consider whether to shorten the procedural timelines to have the application heard and resolved more quickly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have no doubt that the Courts, in applying its discretion to the facts of each case, will have the fair balance between the parties' interests at heart when deciding.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Christopher de Souza asked what steps the agencies will take to avoid or minimise remand where RT is a possible sentence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, as I mentioned earlier, the agencies will work to identify the remand cases where the accused is under the age of 21 early.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This age group includes all accused for whom RT may be ordered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The identification of these cases may be done even before a charge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once such cases are identified, the Prosecution and investigators will take steps to expedite the case and reach the sentencing stage as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, in appropriate cases, remand can be avoided by offering a reduced bail amount, for example, if the sureties have difficulty raising bail in those situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Release on bail with electronic tagging can also be used as an alternative to higher bail amounts, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The CJRA amended the CPC to expressly allow the use of electronic tagging as a condition of bail.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, that will be so, and, in such a situation, it will be started immediately.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Generally, the CPC empowers the Courts to direct a sentence of imprisonment, RT or Corrective Training (CT) or Preventive Detention take effect at a later date than the date it was passed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, however, is usually done on the request of the offender in most of these cases, to allow, for example, time to sort out personal affairs and so on before serving a sentence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the usual position is that if you are already in pre-sentence remand, then unless the offender requests, he will simply carry on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the offender is already in remand in that situation and they are not requesting bail to sort out personal affairs or other matters, then there is generally no reason to postpone the commencement of sentence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As background, although CT sentences share the rehabilitative element with RT, they apply to a different group of offenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government is continuously working towards a progressive, balanced and modern criminal justice system that protects society from crime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill contributes to this effort by building on past reforms and also, at the same time, enhancing their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the support of the House, I beg to move.      .
